body:
# EngineShelf 1.1.6

1.1.5 put four engines on the shelf. This release is what happened when they were
run on the other half of the product: **every job on Windows was running with its
log unreachable**, and the WebKit container was built from a rule about which
Ubuntu image an archive wanted, which is wrong for five of fifty-three rows.

Both were invisible on the machine each was written on. So the release also ships
the four checkers that hold the two halves to each other, and `CLAUDE.md` writes
down the two rules they check.

**Anyone on 1.1.5 should take this.** Its packaged downloads were missing
`lib/engines.sh` / `lib/engines.ps1`, and every entry point sources that file —
see **Fixed**.

## Windows: the manager caught up with the macOS one

The page is one file, `gui/app.js`, served by both managers, and it cannot tell
which one answered. Where it read something only `gui/server.py` sent, the feature
was silently missing on Windows.

- **Every job has a log again.** `/api/doctor-install` answered with a `stream`
  key on Python and without one on PowerShell — and the page takes that key out
  of the answer and polls `/api/log/<key>`. With no key it opens no panel and no
  tab, so *every* job on Windows ran unwatched, most visibly a dependency install,
  which has no progress bar on its row to stand in for the log. `Get-State`
  carried no `logs` at all either, so the page read the manager as older than
  itself and said so in place of every log. There is now a real stream layer in
  `gui/server.ps1`: one log per target with a divider between runs, `/api/logs`
  and `/api/log/<key>`, a tab strip rebuilt from the manager rather than from the
  page's memory — so it survives a reload and shows what the other window is
  doing. Rendered from the job files on demand, because that manager is a single
  thread serving HTTP and there is nobody there to append lines as they arrive.
- **Downloads show progress.** `Invoke-WebRequest` is ~20× slower with its
  progress bar on and prints nothing with it off, so a 60–300 MB download was
  minutes of silence: the row stuck on "installing…", the log empty between
  *Downloading* and *Extracting*. `engineshelf.ps1` now copies the bytes itself
  and prints a meter in the shape the page parses (`OWN_METER` in `app.js`),
  formatted against `InvariantCulture` — with the machine's culture, a Windows set
  to Vietnamese, German or French printed `1,3 GB` and the row went back to having
  no progress at all, on exactly the machines nobody tests on.
- **A job gets nothing on stdin.** `Start-Process` inherits the manager's unless
  told otherwise, and an inherited stdin that never answers is a job that never
  ends — winget waiting on its source agreements, `sudo` waiting on a password
  inside WSL. The log stopped dead after the question and the only way out was
  quitting the manager. Jobs now get an empty file on stdin, the way `server.py`
  gives every child `DEVNULL`, prompts are accepted on the command line as well
  (`--accept-source-agreements --accept-package-agreements --silent`), and a
  **doctor job is cancellable** — the others because calling them off is free,
  this one because there has to be a way out of somebody else's installer.
- **Docker inside WSL 2 is a supported route.** The manager and the launcher work
  out where docker actually is, translate the only two host paths docker is ever
  handed (the Dockerfile and the build context), and the dependency doctor can
  install WSL 2 with an elevation prompt of its own instead of hanging on `sudo`.
- **`Reset the container's profile` is not a dead button.** The page offered it,
  `engineshelf-docker.ps1` implemented `clean`, and the allow-list in
  `gui/server.ps1` did not have the verb — a 400 on Windows only, with nothing to
  say why.
- **Four variables that nothing assigned.** `$Engines` is what the shell twin
  calls the engine list; nothing on the PowerShell side defines it. `$null
  -notcontains 'webkit'` is *true*, so **every** Docker verb died on
  `Unknown engine: <engine>. Known:` with an empty list, and `catalog` listed
  Chromium alone under a footer advertising `run firefox:115`. Indexing `$null`
  throws instead, so eight lines of ordinary output were eight ways to end a
  command in a stack trace after the work was done. All of it goes through
  `Test-EngineKnown` / `Get-EngineDisplay` now, and `tools/check-psvars.ps1` finds
  the next one — it found four, in two files.
- **What a vendor still serves is asked in a child process.** `engineshelf.ps1
  refresh-native` probes downloadability, the WebKit floor and milestone version
  strings, and stores the answer on disk; the manager fires it hidden and reads
  the result on a later poll. On macOS and Linux those probes run on background
  threads, which PowerShell has no counterpart for.

## WebKit: ask the CDN, do not consult a boundary

A WebKit container's base image and its archive are **one** decision. The 22.04
archive on Debian 12 dies at exec on `libicudata.so.70`; the 20.04 archive in a
22.04 image builds cleanly and then dies on `libvpx.so.6`. Ten minutes and a
gigabyte after the button, pointing at nothing.

`WEBKIT_FOCAL_BELOW = 1724` said which side of the line a revision was on.
Measured against the CDN one revision at a time, availability is not a boundary
and not monotonic:

| | |
|---|---|
| r1668, r1715 | no Linux build at all, on any release |
| r1908 | 20.04 only, in the middle of the jammy range |
| r1751, r1944, r1992 | 22.04 only, where their neighbours have both |

So nothing guesses any more. The launchers ask (three HEAD requests, on a path
that is about to download a hundred megabytes from the same CDN), `tools/
discover.py` records the answer per revision as a seventh field on the catalog's
`S` rows, and both managers read it: **the two revisions published for nothing
close the row's Docker route** instead of offering a build that spends a minute on
a base image and then 404s. `Dockerfile.webkit` takes one `UBUNTU` arg that sets
base and archive together, so a mismatched pair cannot be expressed.

**The runtime dependency list is gone too.** There were two hand-written ones,
focal and jammy, and they were wrong the way hand-written lists are always wrong —
quietly, and only for revisions nobody tested. The focal list was measured against
r1446; from r1630 the bundle carries its own libmanette, which links a libevdev
that r1446 never needed, so every one of those revisions died at exec on
`libevdev.so.2`. A missing library is not a build failure: the image builds fine
and the browser is what refuses to start, and it reached the user as "WebKit keeps
failing to start (status 127)". `docker/webkit-deps.sh` replaces both lists with
three layers, cheapest first: the archive's own
`minibrowser-gtk/install-dependencies.sh` (present on every revision the shelf
offers, r1446 to r2336, 113–136 packages, written by the people who compiled it),
then a soname lookup for anything still unresolved, then **failing the build**,
naming the library. A container that cannot start its browser is worth less than
one that was never built, and the difference is which of us finds out.

## The container desktop is the size of your display

The virtual screen has been 1440×900 since the first image, baked into the
Dockerfile, and every desktop is drawn scaled to fit the tab — bars down the
sides on a display of another shape, and the whole desktop rendered smaller than
the window showing it on a bigger one. The manager now starts a container at the
size of the display you are about to look at it on, or at whatever is typed in the
window-size box; from the command line, `--screen 1920x1080` or
`SCREEN=1920x1080`. Clamped, because every pixel of that framebuffer is drawn by
an emulated x86.

It is settled **when the container starts** and cannot change afterwards: Xvfb
fixes its framebuffer at startup, and x11vnc can report a resize the X server made
but cannot be asked for one. Restart the container to change it.

## Cameras, microphones, and the origin they are asked from

"The camera does not work in Docker" was one complaint covering two faults.

- **No device.** Docker Desktop runs the container inside a Linux VM with no USB
  passthrough, so on macOS and Windows a webcam plugged into the machine cannot
  reach it by any route — **test a real camera on the native launcher.** What the
  container does instead is stand in the engine's fake camera, so `getUserMedia`
  resolves and the code under test runs rather than dying on `NotFoundError`.
  Drop a `camera.y4m` in the profile volume and that becomes the camera, looped —
  a QR code, a document, a face. On a Linux host the real `/dev/video*` and
  `/dev/snd` are passed in when they exist and the fake one steps aside.
- **The wrong origin.** A dev server on the host is
  `http://host.docker.internal:<port>`, which is not a secure origin — so
  `navigator.mediaDevices` is simply absent and the page reports "no camera" when
  the real answer is "not localhost". Every port on that host is now treated as
  secure (a hostname pattern, not a list of the dev-server ports somebody thought
  of — measured: a page on `:4291` reported `isSecureContext=false` with the list
  and `true` with the pattern). Firefox has no switch for it, so the two prefs are
  written into its profile on first start and left alone afterwards.
  `INSECURE_ORIGINS` is still the way to name a host reached some other way, an IP
  on the LAN say.

## Cmd-V on a Mac actually pastes

The clipboard bridge had one route to the host clipboard, and on a page whose
focus is always a canvas, Safari and Firefox never fired `paste` — so Cmd-V did
nothing at all. There are three routes now (a hidden textarea focused for the
length of the gesture, the page's own `paste` event, and
`navigator.clipboard.readText`); whichever answers first wins. Ctrl-V is caught as
well, since the desktop on the other side is Linux and that is its paste, but
macOS performs no paste for it — refused clipboard access it pastes the
container's own clipboard and says so. **Cmd-V is the one that always reaches this
machine's clipboard.**

## The job log is coloured

A container build is eight minutes of apt output with four lines in it that anyone
wanted, and every one of those was the same grey. Each line is now read once on
its way into the panel and given one word for what it is: a result, a warning, a
failure, the address the browser came up at, the divider between two runs,
everything else dim. Deliberately a small vocabulary — a log where everything is
highlighted is a log where nothing is.

What it reads is the CLIs' own wording, and **both** halves of every pair: the
shell marks a result `v Chromium 120 ready.` and PowerShell marks it `OK Chromium
120 ready.`. BuildKit's step numbers and timings are stripped before the line is
read, so apt's own `E:` is found where it really is. `tools/check-phases.mjs`
holds both CLIs to all of it.

## The row's button is the shortest way to a browser

A recommendation is not the whole story. A Docker-first row kept the button for
the container even when its image had yet to be built and a native copy was
already on disk — so the row read **Get** over a version that was installed, with
the one thing that could start right now hidden in the menu. The container keeps
the button when its image exists; otherwise the build on disk wins, and the
recommendation stays in the tooltip, the route marks and one click away.

- **Both routes closed means no button at all**, not the other route's button.
  `dockerOnly` is false wherever Docker is missing, so a row with nothing left to
  download used to fall through to the plain native Get — on a row whose own
  tooltip said there was nothing to download. Every Edge row on Windows sits in
  that state, and so does an aged-out Edge or WebKit on a mac.
  `nothingToOffer()` in `app.js` decides it and `tools/check-rows.mjs` pins it.
- **Edge on Windows says the true thing.** The mac wording ("the feed has nothing
  left") reads as *wait for the vendor*. Nothing is missing there and nothing will
  change: Microsoft ships Edge for Windows as an `.msi` that installs no files of
  its own — no File table, a 12-byte Component table, and a 258 MB Binary stream
  whose first two bytes are `MZ`, run by a custom action — so `msiexec /a`
  extracts nothing and there is no Edge archive for Windows anywhere in the feed.
  The container runs the Linux build instead.

## Four checkers, and the rules they check

`CLAUDE.md` now states the two rules the split keeps breaking — *both managers
answer the same page*, *native and Docker offer the same shelf* — and a
divergence is allowed only when it is written down:

```bash
node tools/check-parity.mjs                        # routes, state fields, job fields, verbs
node tools/check-rows.mjs                          # no row offers a button that cannot work
node tools/check-phases.mjs                        # CLI wording <-> what the page parses
pwsh -NoProfile -File tools/check-windows.ps1      # the Windows half, from any machine
```

The last one runs `check-psvars.ps1`, then six suites out of `tools/windows-tests/`
that lift the real functions out of `gui/server.ps1`, `engineshelf.ps1`,
`engineshelf-docker.ps1` and `lib/preflight.ps1` **by parse tree** and run them
against stubs — so what is tested is what ships, and it runs on a mac.
`check-parity.mjs` also fails on an `ALLOWED` entry nobody needs any more, so the
list of permitted differences cannot rot into permission to diverge.

## Fixed

- **The 1.1.5 downloads were missing `lib/engines.sh` and `lib/engines.ps1`.**
  Every entry point sources that file — the CLI, the container launcher and both
  managers — so a downloaded 1.1.5 could not start; `features.tsv` was left out
  too, which turns every row's changelog into `N/A`. `tools/release.sh` copies
  both now. The repo checkout was never affected, which is why it shipped.
- **A scheduled Chromium catalog refresh deleted the other three shelves.**
  `tools/refresh-catalog.py` builds its output from scratch and truncates
  `catalog.tsv`, and it did not read back the `S` rows it does not own — so on the
  run of 2026-08-31 all 288 shelf rows went. `tools/sync-landing.py` then
  republished the landing page from the emptied catalog: no Firefox, Edge or
  WebKit timeline at all and a hero counting zero versions. It had printed a
  warning about exactly that and written anyway; a warning is not a guard when
  the caller is a cron job. The refresh now carries foreign rows across verbatim,
  and the sync **refuses** to publish an empty shelf.
- **The Windows manager could not start on a machine without Docker.** A bare
  `docker` call throws `CommandNotFoundException`, which `2>$null` does not catch,
  and this one ran at startup outside any request handler.
- **`tools/obfuscate.sh` orphaned block comments.** Stripping `#`-leading lines
  took the opening `<#` of a `<# … #>` block and left the closer behind, so a
  release-built `.ps1` could fail to parse. Blocks are dropped whole now.
- Docker actions for a selector no image understands are refused up front rather
  than failing with the reason buried in a job log.

## Upgrading

- **Rebuild WebKit containers.** The base image is chosen per revision now, and an
  image built by 1.1.5 may be the wrong pair — the one that builds and then dies
  at exec. `./engineshelf-docker.sh rebuild webkit:16.4`, or **Rebuild image** in
  the row's menu.
- **Windows, Docker inside WSL:** nothing to do, but the dependency doctor will
  now offer to finish an incomplete WSL 2 install instead of hanging.
- Everything else needs nothing: extract over the old copy and start it. Browsers
  and profiles are untouched.

Artifacts: `EngineShelf-1.1.6-macOS.zip`, `EngineShelf-1.1.6-Windows.zip`,
`EngineShelf-1.1.6-Linux.tar.gz`. Verify with `SHA256SUMS.txt`.
